summary:
NASA Mission Control Simulator allows you to step into the shoes of a mission planner and look at some of the challenges that are based on actual space science. You can rotate the 3D Earth, go through various missions (climate monitoring, lunar and Mars exploration, asteroid awareness, deep space observation etc) and then look at the objectives and constraints of each mission.

The project is all about making space exploration feel tangible and hands on. Rather than just reading about the missions you can actually go into the problems that a spacecraft team might face and work through them. It's also a way of learning and exploring together with co-op and progress tracking.

The aim is to get people interested in space science and to demonstrate how the data, planning and engineering all come together in a mission.
details:
Project Summary

NASA Mission Control Simulator is an interactive, web-based aerospace engineering experience inspired by the NASA Systems Engineering Handbook and GMAT (General Mission Analysis Tool). It lets users design, validate, and operate simulated space missions while considering engineering constraints such as spacecraft mass margins, electrical power budgets, telemetry link budgets, and orbital mechanics.

Core Features and Systems

Interactive 3D CAD Design Studio
Assemble spacecraft in a live 3D environment, from CubeSats to flagship-class observatories. Components include PBR (physically based rendering) materials, solar arrays, radioisotope thermoelectric generators (RTGs), chemical and ion thrusters, and scientific payloads.

Launch and Ascent
Simulate a multistage rocket launch from Kennedy Space Center Launch Complex 39A (LC-39A), including stage separation and a Mach 1.0 condensation vapor cone.

Orbital Operations and Houston Mission Control
Monitor a real-time 2D Mercator ground track and simulated AOS/LOS (acquisition/loss of signal) coverage from Goldstone, Madrid, Canberra, Wallops, and Svalbard tracking stations. The console includes rolling telemetry oscilloscope charts and Keplerian delta-v orbital maneuvers.

Red Pioneer: Four-Phase Mars Mission

  1. Earth launch and Trans-Mars Injection (TMI): Perform an escape burn of approximately 3,800 m/s, with characteristic energy C₃ > 0 km²/s².
  2. Deep-space cruise: Travel approximately 225 million km on a heliocentric trajectory while accounting for DSN signal delay and declining solar flux, from 1,361 W/m² to 590 W/m².
  3. Mars Entry, Descent, and Landing (EDL): Simulate hypersonic heat-shield plasma effects, supersonic parachute deployment, and rocket-powered sky-crane descent.
  4. Jezero Crater exploration: Drive a six-wheel rover, drill rock cores, and use Raman/PIXL spectroscopic analysis to search for potential ancient biosignatures.

Multiplayer and Technology

Collaborative crew rooms support roles such as Flight Director, Systems Engineer, Science Lead, and Communications Officer, with state synchronized using WebSockets.

The frontend uses Vanilla JavaScript (ES6+), HTML5 Canvas 2D, and CSS3. Three.js provides WebGL-based 3D graphics, including PBR shaders and a Rayleigh atmosphere shader. The backend uses Node.js and WebSockets (ws); KaTeX renders mathematical notation. The site is deployed through Vercel’s CDN.

NASA Data and References

The project references NASA Blue Marble and Black Marble imagery, Deep Space Network station information, the NASA Systems Engineering Handbook (NASA/SP-2016-6105 Rev. 2), Mars 2020 Perseverance mission architecture and Jezero Crater geology, and JPL Horizons planetary ephemerides and orbital mechanics constants.

Live demo: nasa-hazel.vercel.app
